name: Argentina
summary: A South American republic that declared independence from Spain in 1816. In the early 20th century it was one of the richest countries in the world; later it went through coups, debt crises and recovery.

knownFor.label: Tango
knownFor.note: A dance and music born in the port neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

knownFor.label: Gauchos
knownFor.note: Horse-riding cattle herders of the pampas, also important as soldiers in the independence wars.

knownFor.label: Asado
knownFor.note: Beef grilled over wood fire, part of national life.

location.value: Southern South America, from the subtropical north to Tierra del Fuego; about 2.8 million km².

terrain.value: The fertile Pampas plains, the Andes in the west (Aconcagua, the highest peak in the Americas), Patagonia in the south.

climate.value: Temperate in the Pampas; subtropical in the north; cold and windy in Patagonia.

resources.value: Some of the best farmland in the world, cattle, wheat, soybeans, lithium, and shale gas (Vaca Muerta).

disasters.value: Floods on the Pampas, droughts, and earthquakes in the Andes (San Juan, 1944).

population.value: About 1.8 million in 1869; about 46 million today.

urbanisation.value: Highly urban; about a third of people live in Greater Buenos Aires.

disease.value: Yellow fever in Buenos Aires (1871) killed about 8% of the city.

migration.value: Huge immigration from Italy and Spain (about 6 million arrivals, 1857–1930).

economicBase.value: Exports of beef, wheat and wool; later industry; today soybeans, cars and energy.

tradeRoutes.value: Railways (many British-built) carried crops to the port of Buenos Aires for Europe.

wealth.value: Among the world’s richest countries around 1900–1914; repeated crises since.

moneyAndTax.value: Several currencies; high inflation and defaults (1989, 2001); the peso was pegged to the dollar 1991–2001.

inequality.value: Land was concentrated in large estates (estancias); workers’ movements grew in the 20th century.

governmentType.value: A federal presidential republic; interrupted by military coups (1930, 1955, 1966, 1976).

keyRulers.value: José de San Martín (independence). Domingo Sarmiento. Juan Perón and Eva Perón. Raúl Alfonsín. Néstor and Cristina Kirchner. Javier Milei.

succession.value: Elections, often interrupted by coups until 1983; democracy since then.

institutions.value: The 1853 constitution, Congress, provinces, the Supreme Court.

stability.value: Civil wars in the 19th century; the last military dictatorship (1976–83) caused the “disappearance” of thousands of people (estimates range from about 9,000 to 30,000).

eliteConflict.value: Long conflict between Buenos Aires and the provinces; later between Peronists and anti-Peronists.

armyAndTech.value: Armies of independence (San Martín crossed the Andes in 1817).

majorWars.value: Wars of independence; the War of the Triple Alliance against Paraguay (1864–70); the Falklands War with Britain (1982).

territoryChange.value: Took Patagonia from Indigenous peoples in the “Conquest of the Desert” (1878–85).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivalries with Brazil and Chile; founding member of Mercosur (1991).

inventions.value: Fingerprint classification for police (Vucetich, 1891), the ballpoint pen (developed by Bíró in Buenos Aires, 1943), the bus (colectivo).

scienceEducation.value: Free public education (1884 law); Nobel prizes in science (Houssay, Leloir, Milstein).

openness.value: Very open to immigration and trade before 1930; more protectionist after.

religion.value: Mainly Catholic; Pope Francis (elected 2013) was Argentine.

artsArchitecture.value: Tango, the writer Jorge Luis Borges, Buenos Aires architecture, football.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class for Latin America, but rising poverty during crises.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong sense of national identity built on immigration, the gaucho and the Malvinas/Falklands claim.

neighbours.value: Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay.

ideasReligions.value: Liberal ideas from Europe; later Peronism, a movement mixing nationalism and workers’ rights.

colonisation.value: Claims the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), held by Britain since 1833.

riseSignals.value: The May Revolution (1810) in Buenos Aires and independence (1816) from Spain.

peakPeriod.value: The “golden age” of farm exports, about 1880–1914.

declineSignals.value: Political instability, coups and repeated debt crises after 1930.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Argentina; Wikipedia: History of Argentina.

overallCertainty.value: Well documented; numbers of victims of the dictatorship are disputed.
